title: Sandwich-generation caregiving compresses complex care, paid work, and family life into the same hours
source_unit: AARP Public Policy Institute and National Alliance for Caregiving, Caught in the Middle: The Crucial Role of Sandwich Generation Caregivers, part of the Caregiving in the US 2025 series
geography: United States; family caregivers of adults with complex medical conditions or disabilities who are also raising children

denominator.unit: adult family caregivers caring for an adult while raising children

share_of_adult_caregivers.unit: percent of caregivers of an adult

observations.method: AARP/National Alliance for Caregiving Caregiving in the US 2025 survey series, with a dedicated analysis of caregivers simultaneously raising children and caring for an adult with a complex medical condition or disability.
observations.uncertainty: The source describes a survey-defined caregiving population and does not establish that sandwich status caused any reported work, health, or financial outcome; counts depend on caregiving and child-rearing definitions.
observations.subgroup: Adult family caregivers who are raising children while caring for an adult with complex medical needs or a disability.
observations.counterinterpretation: The overlap can reflect life-course timing, family preference, cultural obligation, or available formal care as well as inadequate support; the population estimate does not measure unmet need by itself.

observations.period: 2025 caregiving survey; weekly care and task intensity

denominator.unit: sandwich-generation caregivers and other adult caregivers

weekly_care_hours.unit: average hours per week for sandwich-generation caregivers; about the same as other caregivers

high_intensity_care.unit: percent of sandwich-generation caregivers, versus 36% of other caregivers

medical_or_nursing_tasks.unit: percent of sandwich-generation caregivers, versus 53% of other caregivers

observations.method: Descriptive subgroup comparisons from the Caregiving in the US 2025 survey series; intensity combines hours and assistance with complex daily or medical tasks as defined by the source.
observations.uncertainty: Equal average hours do not mean equal burden: task complexity, scheduling, child needs, paid work, travel, and care-recipient condition are not fully represented by the weekly-hour comparison.
observations.subgroup: Sandwich-generation caregivers compared with other caregivers of adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: The higher-intensity pattern may partly reflect differences in the conditions of care recipients or in who identifies as a caregiver, rather than a general effect of raising children.

observations.period: 2025 caregiving survey; health, work, and financial consequences

physical_strain_relative_risk.value: 50% higher risk of physical strain than other caregivers

work_disruption.unit: percent reporting a work disruption due to caregiving

provider_asked_caregiver_needs.unit: percent who had ever been asked by a health care provider what they needed to care for themselves

observations.method: Subgroup estimates from the Caregiving in the US 2025 survey series covering caregiver-reported physical, employment, financial, and health-system contact experiences.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported, cross-sectional associations; work disruption and financial strain are not broken into hours, earnings, debt, job exit, or employer support, and provider contact does not measure the adequacy of any help received.
observations.subgroup: Sandwich-generation caregivers; comparisons are with other adult caregivers where the source reports them.
observations.counterinterpretation: Families may absorb disruption through flexible work, kin support, savings, or reduced consumption; reported strain does not show which coping route was chosen or whether it lasted.

related_sources.claim: Official DOI citation for the report, published September 15, 2026.

boundary: This record adds a life-course and household-capacity layer to the care stream: sandwich-generation caregivers are a large population that compresses complex adult care and child-rearing into overlapping time, work, health, and financial obligations. It does not establish causality, care adequacy, household trajectories, or the effects of any specific policy or employer intervention.
